articles.title: Save $200 Off Sonos' Best Dolby Atmos Soundbar
articles.summary: It even has a built-in subwoofer so you can skip buying a separate one.
articles.body:
If you're looking to upgrade your home theater system to a Dolbty Atmos setup but you're looking for sleek and minimalist, then don't miss out this Sonos deal today. Amazon is currently offering the flagship Sonos Arc Ultra Dolby Atmos soundbar for $899 with free shipping after a $200 instant discount. This is Sonos' best soundbar and even has a built-in subwoofer if you want to forego the cost and hassle of buying a seaparate one.

Save $200 Off the Sonos Arc Ultra Soundbar

Given the number of upgrades, the Sonos Arc Ultra should be considered more as a new class of flagship soundbar than a mere update of the original Arc. At first glance, both look similar, with the same 46" long profile, but the internals are totally different. Whereas the Arc featured a 5.0.2ch setup with eleven speakers and no sub, the Arc Ultra boasts an expanded 9.4.1ch setup with fourteen speakers including a four-motor, dual-membrane Sound Motion woofer for better bass response and low end. It's a big improvement over the previous generation Sonos Arc and just about every other soundbar in it price range. Fair disclosure, you'll still get noticeably more powerful low-end performance with a standalone sub, but not everyone needs the extra power or wants the hassle and expense that comes with adding in a second speaker.

The Arc Ultra also supports Dolby Atmos thanks to two dedicated up-firing tweeters for spatial audio and new AI enhancement technology to isolate and boost the clarity of dialogue and voices. It has a built-in microphone so that it can be controlled using voice commands using your favorite smart assistant. Check out our own Sonos Arc Ultra review .

articles.title: Crimson Desert Is Becoming Crimson Desert Enhanced for Free
articles.summary: Pearl Abyss has announced Crimson Desert Enhanced, a new version of the game with additional story, available free to all players.
articles.body:
Pearl Abyss has announced Crimson Desert Enhanced , a new version of the game with additional story, available free to all players.

Simply update the game to version 2.00.00 and Crimson Desert Enhanced will be yours, Pearl Abyss has aid. So, to be clear, it is just a fresh patch for the existing game — but one that Pearl Abyss feels is so substantial that it warrants an updated title for the full game.

Crimson Desert Enhanced adds new cutscenes and story moments throughout the main questline, plus voiceover support so you can enjoy the game's narrative in German, French, Spanish, Brazilian Portuguese and Japanese.

Pearl Abyss previously promised a summer roadmap of content that includes improvements to the core narrative – a recurring criticism of the game at launch. And of course, the Enhanced edition will include all existing updates to the game — and there have been a lot, with new bits and pieces every few weeks.

All of this comes ahead of the game's first paid DLC, due this year, and a Nintendo Switch 2 release, expected in early 2027. Research on multiplayer modes and potential sequels is also underway , following the game's breakout success so far.

Crimson Desert launched back in March 19 and was an instant hit for Pearl Abyss. Less than three months after launch, Crimson Desert crossed the 6 million copies sold mark .

Catch up on all of tonight's announcements in our roundup of everything revealed at Gamescom Opening Night Live 2026 .

articles.title: Backrooms Is Officially Coming to HBO Max in September
articles.summary: Backrooms officially has a streaming release date.
articles.body:
Backrooms officially has a streaming release date.

The breakout horror movie directed by 21-year-old-Kane Parsons is coming to HBO Max on Friday, September 25. It will debut on HBO linear channels the following day at 8pm ET.

The streaming release comes just under four months after Backrooms was initially released in theaters, where it dominated the box office. It grossed over $80 million in its opening weekend and quickly become A24’s highest-grossing movie of all time . It finished its theatrical run at just shy of $400 million globally , and remains one of the highest-grossing movies of the year so far .

Toward the end of its stint in theaters, Backrooms received became available to watch in extended “Everything Must Go” screenings, featuring over 15 minutes of extra footage in the style of Parsons’ original YouTube series. That extra footage is already available to watch on YouTube for free , and it's unclear whether it'll be added to HBO Max in any capacity.

For now, Backrooms is available to rent or buy digitally from platforms like Prime Video. A spread of 4K Blu-rays with "over three hours of special features" are also available to buy from the A24 Shop .

We were pretty big fans of Backrooms, with critic Lex Briscuso describing it as “a truly terrifying cinematic rabbit hole” in her 8/10 review for IGN . It's one of our best-reviewed movies of the year so far, and generally currently sits at an 87% rating on Rotten Tomatoes .

All in all, it should come as no surprise that there are already talks of a potential sequel , though Parsons has also expressed his interest in adapting the iconic 2007 Valve game, Portal. Other creepypasta-inspired movies have also been getting the green light since the Backrooms success, most notably a Siren Head movie helmed by Weapons ' and the upcoming Resident Evil movie's director, Zach Cregger.

articles.title: Path of Exile 2 Release Date Sets 1.0 Launch in December 2026
articles.summary: Grinding Gear Games has announced Path of Exile 2 1.0 has a December release date.
articles.body:
Grinding Gear Games has announced Path of Exile 2 1.0 has a December release date.

The studio announced the long-awaited schedule update with a trailer that premiered at gamescom Opening Night Live (ONL) 2026, confirming plans to bring its free-to-play action-RPG to PC via Steam and the Epic Games Store, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S December 11, 2026. The footage mixed together Path of Exile 2 gameplay with cinematics while promising that players will finally get their hands on a complete build just in time for the holidays.

Grinding Gear revealed more information on its website , directing interested fans to register for more information. Those who do can unlock exclusive rewards.

"Path of Exile 2 is a next-generation action RPG from Grinding Gear Games, featuring co-op for up to six players," an official description on its Steam page said. "Path of Exile 2 takes place in the land of Wraeclast, a dark continent populated by unique cultures, ancient secrets, and monstrous dangers. A sinister threat, long thought destroyed, has begun creeping back on the edge of civilisation, driving people mad and sickening the land with Corruption."

Grinding Gear first launched Path of Exile 2 in an early access state in December 2024. All the buildup led to a massive launch on Steam , and now, after a few years of ups and downs , the full launch will finally bring the team's vision for launch to life. Part of that vision includes the Duelist, a new class showcased in today's trailer that will be available at launch.

IGN called Path of Exile 2 early access "Great" in our 8/10 review . Even in its unrefined state at the time, we said its "redefined action and surprisingly fleshed-out endgame" got things off to a good start. While we wait for updates, be sure to check out everything announced at gamescom ONL 2026 .

articles.title: LEGO Skylines Announced at Gamescom
articles.summary: A new LEGO city builder known as LEGO Skylines has been announced at Gamescom.
articles.body:
A new LEGO city builder known as LEGO Skylines has been announced at Gamescom.

After a leak earlier this summer , Paradox Interactive has officially announced a LEGO version of its beloved city builder series, Cities: Skylines. Developed by Iceflake Studios, LEGO Skylines aims to allow players to build functional and logical cities, as you would in other city builders, but also push them to make something more creative and whimsical. One such example provided by the team behind the game is putting a bakery on every corner of the city, which can produce donuts using wheat provided by farmers from elsewhere in your city.

Using the creativity and imagination of the LEGO brand, LEGO Skylines players will be able to build the city of their dreams — not just maintain a realistic, functioning city, but one that lets them try outlandish and absurd ideas using LEGO bricks and decorations. The game promises a "frankly absurd amount of buildings, decorations, and other cool stuff" to build cities.

“Building and creativity have always been at the heart of the LEGO experience, but LEGO Skylines takes us into completely new territory,” said Fredrik Löving, SVP, Global Head of game at the LEGO Group. “Together with Paradox Interactive and Iceflake Studios, we have brought the LEGO experience to one of the world's most beloved gaming genres. From the beginning, our ambition wasn’t just to make a LEGO city-builder, it was to create a game that is considered among the best in the genre. Whether players dream of building a bustling metropolis, a quirky seaside town, or something nobody has imagined before, LEGO Skylines gives them the creative freedom and depth to make it happen.”

All in all, it sounds like a really charming and fun city builder. There's no release date for LEGO Skylines at the moment, but it will be available on Xbox Series X|S, PS5, Nintendo Switch 2, and PC when it comes out.

articles.title: Roco Kingdom Goes Global
articles.body:
Since its launch in China in March 2026, Roco Kingdom has made a huge mark on the country's app charts. The game went straight to the top among new mobile titles, both in terms of average daily active users and revenue. Revealed at Gamescom Opening Night Live 2026, Morefun Studios will be bringing this hugely popular Chinese franchise to the rest of the world with their first global closed beta test on 27th October.

If you've never heard of Roco Kingdom, that's because the franchise has spent most of its 16-year life in China, where it's seen huge success. What started as a browser game in 2010 has since spawned four feature films, a long-running animated series, and over 100 published books. The game itself has had more than 350 million registered players across its history.

Roco Kingdom is a multiplayer open-world creature-collecting game where players take on the role of a Roco, setting out to explore the sprawling continent of Carosia to befriend its native creatures, called Jinies. There are over 400+ of them at launch, and no two are quite the same: every Jini has its own unique height, weight, and habits, interacting with the world around them in ways that make the environment feel variable and dynamic.

Developed by Morefun Studios, known for extraction shooter Arena Breakout: Infinite, the latest game has been in development for the last six years. The world itself is built around natural habitats, with distinct landscapes and climates shaping where different Jini species live and behave with the outcome being a living ecosystem rather than a static backdrop.

Meet, Bond, and Journey Together With Friends

The creature-collecting loop will feel familiar to anyone who's spent time with the genre: discover Jinies in the wild, catch them, and build a roster. But Roco Kingdom’s 16-year heritage allows it to build on its significant foundations. The social systems here go beyond simply trading and battling: players can decorate and farm their own home spaces, visit friends' setups, and hop on shared rides together through the world. Cross-platform play is supported, meaning PC players and mobile players can journey through Carosia side by side.

With regards to the PvP system, whilst the game is free-to-play, Morefun Studios are at pains to state that this isn’t simply a case of pay to win. Every Jini is obtainable through gameplay, and the competitive meta is built entirely around strategy; type matchups, team composition, and roster diversity rather than just how much you've spent.

If you’d like to get a taste of the full kingdom, check out their reveal trailer here:

Roco Kingdom launches its first closed beta test on 27th October, on PC, iOS and Android. Registration is now open via rocokingdom.com . Stay tuned to IGN as more about the game is revealed in the coming months.

articles.title: 1001 Threads of Mizan: The First Preview
articles.summary: While I can definitely see it working well solo, playing with two other players in real time is where 1001 Threads of Mizan really shines. There were no multiplayer quick time events or big flashy mid-fight cutscenes that triggered when everyone did a specific thing, but there were definitely moments where all three of us needed to attack a single weak point, or work together to defeat various obstacles at once in different areas during the boss fight. I'm very interested to see how this fusion of single-player and co-op works throughout the game.
articles.body:
GTA 6 isn’t even out yet and 2026 has already been a great year for video games. From this spring's outstanding Resident Evil Requiem to surprises like Denshattack, Mina The Hollower, and other games like 007, Life is Strange Reunion, Marathon… you get the point. This year has been awesome, so the bar is a little high for me when it comes to playing something original from a brand new studio like MBC. 1001 Threads of Mizan is a completely original title from a new studio led by a plethora of industry veterans who are looking to make something that not only brings the world and stories of One Thousand and One Nights to an action-adventure game, but also create something that plays as fun as it looks. And from my short time with iit, fighting two bosses and zipping around on a magic carpet, I can definitely see the vision — and in an era of games that are constantly redefining what it means to be great, 1001 Threads of Mizan is looking pretty promising.

From the very start of my demo it was obvious that 1001 Threads of Mizan’s developer MBC Game Studio is taking its source material seriously in an effort to make something that’s unique and interesting. After the intro cutscene, there was barely any chatter between the three main characters, and most of the world-building and story was handled by a narrator, Shahrazad, who is the actual storyteller in the book One Thousand and One Nights that 1001 Threads of Mizan is based on. 1001 Threads is rich with its source material, and it was great seeing an action-adventure game take place in a time period that isn't really covered that often in AAA games.

But story isn't everything, and in my short time with 1001 Threads of Mizan, it was obvious that the gameplay falls somewhere between Kingdom Hearts’ fast-paced and flashy combat and a souls-like approach to pattern recognition and dodging. Mizan is a really fun game, and in my demo I was able to fight numerous Jinn enemies, as well as two interesting and surprisingly challenging boss battles. One of which took a bit more teamwork to take down than I had anticipated, which was really fun and took me back to the good ol’ days of couch co-op games with my friends.

In my demo, I was given a choice between three distinct characters who play within their classes. Yusra is based on more long-range weapons and attacks, while Malik is your typical heavy who deals high damage at close range and can be a bit of a tank, while Sufyan plays a bit faster. I chose Sufyan and immediately figured out his playstyle without the need of a complicated tutorial system or overbearing menus. Everything just seemed to click, and I never had to take a beat to figure out how to play the game. The combat felt tight and responsive, dodging and blocking felt natural, and managing my special attack meter was easy and quickly became second nature.

1001 Threads of Mizan - First Screenshots

The real star of the show here, though, is the ability to auto-summon a magic carpet anywhere and zip around the environment. This was great to use in combat if I needed to get away from the action to recover, get closer to an enemy's weak spot, or just use it to help juggle aerial combos and perform team-based attacks. The magic carpet, like Mizan's combat, just works. It's not overly complicated, it can be summoned with one button, and there was never a moment where I felt like the carpet was moving too fast or clunky. In short, it's a really fun way to move around.

I was told by the game’s directors that 1001 Threads of Mizan is at its core a single-player experience that features a drop-in and drop-out multiplayer aspect. While I can definitely see it working well solo, playing with two other players in real time is where 1001 Threads really shines. There were no multiplayer quick time events or big flashy mid-fight cutscenes that triggered when everyone did a specific thing, but there were definitely moments where all three of us needed to attack a single weak point, or work together to defeat various obstacles at once in different areas during the boss fight. I'm very interested to see how this fusion of single-player and co-op works throughout the game.

In my short time with 1001 Threads of Mizan, it was obvious that this is definitely something worth keeping on your radar thanks to its intuitive and fun combat, a unique take on One Thousand and One Nights, and its take on making a game work as a single-player and multiplayer narrative experience. We’ll have to see how things shake out, but if MBC Game Studio can pull it off, 1001 Threads of Mizan could definitely be one of the most pleasant gaming surprises in quite a while.

articles.title: Gears of War: E-Day Campaign Hands-On Preview: To Quote Marcus Fenix, “Nice”
articles.summary: I’m now not only more fired up to finish Gears of War: E-Day’s prequel story than ever, but I’m also more confident than ever that, at least based on the small slice I’ve played so far, E-Day has struck the exact right balance of tried-and-true old stuff and compelling new stuff.
articles.body:
Playing the beginning of Act 2 of Gears of War: E-Day's campaign immediately gave me a healthy dose of everything I love about Gears of War.

Weapon and combat mechanics have been nicely evolved through the weapon mod system.

Gears 5's open-world aspects have been reined in with something smarter: a multi-path downtown area with optional secondary objectives and plenty of hidden collectibles.

[ Editor's Note : Mild spoilers ahead for E-Day’s campaign, so turn back now if you don’t want to know any more…]

I’m a massive fan of Gears of War, as I have been since the very beginning. But I have to be honest: something about Gears of War: E-Day’s campaign reveal at the Xbox Showcase a couple months ago just didn’t quite land right with me. It wasn’t bad, by any stretch of the imagination. But I just wasn’t as fired up as I thought I’d be after seeing the first new Gears of War campaign footage in seven years (OK, six if we’re counting Hivebusters).

When I finally sat down to play E-Day’s campaign, though, it took all of about 30 seconds to turn my tepid feelings into joyful smiles. My one-hour preview, which covered the early parts of Act 2, featured plenty of everything I want from and love about Gears of War: Marcus Fenix, Dominic Santiago, lots of story cutscenes, a sweet mix of old weapons and new ones (including the origin story for a signature Gears firearm known for its sharp teeth), some evolved gameplay mechanics, killer setpieces, new Marcus Fenix one-liners, subtle references to characters we know and love, and did I mention Marcus Fenix saying and doing cool sh*t?

I was so fired up by what I played that when I got hit with the “demo complete” screen it actually hurt. I suppose The Coalition got the reaction it wanted from me, because all I wanted to do was keep going. And I’m now not only more fired up to finish Gears of War: E-Day’s prequel story than ever, but I’m also more confident than ever that, at least based on the small slice I’ve played so far, E-Day has struck the exact right balance of tried-and-true old stuff and compelling new stuff.

Act 2 picks up with Marcus and Dom still in their civvies, scavenged Mark-1 Lancers in hand. They’ve arrived with fellow civilian-dressed COG soldiers Carter and Reyes at a makeshift command center with the mayor of Kolona, whom they’ve no doubt rescued in Act 1. COG officer Colonel Trench and the mayor face off about whatever the heck is happening out there – you and I both know darn well what it is, of course – and how best to handle it, leading the angry Colonel to yell at our heroes to get some armor on. And then Awesome Moment #1 happens: Marcus and Dom suit up in their familiar COG garb, flanked by Carter and Reyes in the newly christened Bravo Squad. “Guess we’re back to it,” Marcus says, and he might as well be speaking for players as well. My grin could not have been any wider.

Venturing out into the city of Kolona, we see ash raining from a cloudy sky and remnants of once-proud buildings around us. This moment definitely hearkens back to the “destroyed beauty” aesthetic of Gears 1. We soon find our way to the heart of this chapter of gameplay: a massive suspension bridge that raises and lowers in multiple sections in order to let large ships pass underneath it. All of that was in the Before Times, of course, before actual Hell started erupting from the ground beneath the people of this city. We’re making our way towards Oria Stadium, home of the Kolona Eagles thrashball team, where civilians are being routed to in the event of the citywide disaster. But we’re going to have to fight our way there.

This straight-ahead bridge section certainly isn’t the combat bowls we’re used to with Gears, but it’s a great way to warm up – not to mention climb up, meaning: to get a feel for using E-Day’s new verticality, i.e. you can now mantle up and over cover, including the cars that the Locust are using to shield themselves. The Mark-1 Lancer, Gnasher shotgun, Snub pistol, and frag grenades all work exactly as you remember them. Gears of War’s core combat has aged remarkably well over the past 20 years. However, E-Day introduces a welcome new evolution in the form of unlockable weapon mods. Each firearm has four total mod slots, and mods vary by weapon, of course. Every reloadable weapon, by default, gets the classic damage bonus if you nail a perfect reload; it’s called Full Metal Jacket now. But there’s a heck of a lot more than just that. For instance, on the aforementioned Gnasher – which, yes, is still your best point-blank bet for turning low-level Locust Drones into chunky-style soup – has an Auto Pouch mod that automatically reloads the shotgun when you stow it (i.e. switch weapons).

This also seems like a good time to mention the new Tactical Gear, which I unlocked at the very end of my demo build. (You got to experience these in the Versus beta weekend, if you participated.) These are short-duration (45-second) buffs with a cooldown, and they also have unlockable mod slots, none of which were available in the preview. But even without mods, the Adrenaline Injector immediately refills your health when triggered and also increases your damage dealt while decreasing damage taken. Choosing the Sonic Disruptor Tactical Gear, meanwhile, nets you a more defensive bonus: stunning low-level enemies in a cone in front of you, interrupting their attacks. With tons more of all of these left to unlock over the course of the campaign, they should add a welcome bit of personalization and gameplay customization to your playthroughs – emphasis on plural there, because I’ll be shocked if there isn’t a New Game+ available that lets you run the campaign again with all of your Tactical Gear and weapon mods available from the jump on higher difficulties.

After battling our way up and across the massive Allfather’s Legacy Bridge, including fending off a couple of Boomers along the way and getting some reps in with the Breechshot (last seen in Gears of War: Judgment), we arrived at Oria Stadium, where the COG was coordinating a stressful civilian rescue operation, with lines of the city’s residents waiting to be processed and allowed into the massive facility. We entered and caught up with the quartermaster, Russ, who took a liking to Marcus because he knew his father, Adam. He asked what Bravo Squad needed, and after Marcus complained about the bayonets easily breaking off of the Mark-1 Lancers, that’s when one of the COG in our party set the chainsaw used to save Marcus’ life in Act 1, as seen in the Xbox Showcase demo, on the table. The quartermaster looks at the chainsaw with a twinkle in his eye, and, yeah…you can probably see where this is going. Awesome Moment #2: Marcus and Bravo Squad get handed the first prototype Mark-2 Lancers with chainsaw built right in. Again, the smile on my face was almost Joker-like.

We headed out from the stadium with the goal of getting across the downtown section of the city to the train station. It’s here that Awesome Moment #3 began to unfold: environmental freedom. The linear path of the bridge we’d fought across had finally given way to a larger combat space. This seems to deliberately rein in Gears 5’s huge open-world areas by instead giving you room to clear Kalona’s streets block-by-block in whatever order and fashion you choose. It’s a smaller-scale version of what we got in the last game, but based on my initial impression, it’s a more effective one. In fact, I ran through the preview build again to take a different route through Kolona, and I’m glad I did. This approach also allows for higher hidden-collectible potential (because yes, of course there are collectibles in a Gears campaign). I also enjoyed the optional secondary objectives in this section that you can opt into. In one, a family was trapped inside a convenience store, and I had to fight off a wave of Wretches before finding a way inside to free them and radio in to get them an escort to the stadium.

This was also when E-Day introduced Supply Caches, which will be scattered throughout the city and allow you to change out your weapons and mods. It’s an organic and straightforward way of letting you change up weapons on the fly without having to kill an enemy to get what you’re after.

Don’t Need No Credit Card to Ride This Train

The all-too-soon end of my demo came in the Octus Way train station. This was a pretty sizable combat bowl, with three levels of verticality to contend with plus a left, right, and center area of the room to be keeping an eye on, lest the Locust manage to flank you from the side or from behind. It was a frantic but not overwhelming fight; we didn’t face off against the Corpser that was teased while we were clearing Kolona city blocks on our way to the train station, meaning that encounter is no doubt waiting for us later. But Octus Way Station was a good chance to try out all of the weapons (thanks to the Supply Cache in the corner of the upstairs entrance) and rev up the Lancer’s chainsaw for a few good ol’ fashioned Locust executions. Once I loaded up and stepped out of the cleared-out train station, that’s when I got the aforementioned “demo complete” message and reluctantly put down my controller.

One final note: as I mentioned, I ran through the preview twice – once on Performance graphics mode, and once on the 30fps Quality graphics mode. The latter was not running well on Xbox Series X in the preview build. It wasn’t unplayably bad by any means, but it was noticeably sub-30 in a lot of spots. I expect most people will opt for Performance mode anyway, but it’s worth noting and hoping that The Coalition is able to squeeze a few extra fps out of it in the remaining few weeks of development.

That minor complaint aside, I can’t say enough about how much I loved what I’ve played of Gears of War: E-Day’s campaign so far. Does it completely rewrite the rules of Gears? No, but I don’t think anyone – myself included – is looking for that. Besides, this prequel was never about that. It’s about getting Marcus and Dom back together and getting Gears back to its roots. And in the incredibly short slice I’ve seen so far, it absolutely accomplishes that with the highest of marks. I am now chock-full of the hype that the Xbox Showcase demo failed to give me. In the words of Marcus Fenix, sweet .

While you're here, check out these previews of other big upcoming games we've played recently!

Ryan McCaffrey is IGN's executive editor of previews and host of IGN's weekly Xbox show, Podcast Unlocked , and a co-host of Next-Gen Console Watch . He's a North Jersey guy, so it's "Taylor ham," not "pork roll." Debate it with him on Twitter at @DMC_Ryan .

articles.title: The Witcher 3 Remastered Launches September as a Free Upgrade for Existing Owners
articles.summary: CD Projekt Red has announced The Witcher 3 Remastered, coming as a free upgrade to all owners next month.
articles.body:
CD Projekt Red has announced The Witcher 3 Remastered , coming as a free upgrade to all owners on PC, PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S next month on September 29.

In a stunning conclusion to Gamescom's Opening Night Live, the developer confirmed a list of additional features coming to the game's Remastered version as well as notably enhanced visuals, which we've listed out below.

There's no upgrade to the game's current Switch 1 version, though a separate Switch 2-native version of The Witcher 3 Remastered will be sold, and owners of the Switch 1 version will be able to claim this free. The remastered game will also be sold on PC via Battle.net for the first time, where it will unlock a Geralt-themed skin in Diablo 4.

The Witcher 3 Remastered — and the current game, as of today — will also include access to the game's first two expansions at no additional cost. Of course, all of this precedes the arrival of the upcoming Songs of the Past , The Witcher 3's third expansion, due in 2027. For a detailed look at what we saw of that this evening, we have you covered right here .

Everything new coming to The Witcher 3 Remastered

Major features include tweaked combat, improved traversal and movement, revamped mount handling, enhanced monster behaviors, a skill tree revamp, armor transmog, an expanded photo mode, new finishers and much more.

Other additions include the long-awaited cross-platform mod support, new quest tracking, immersive meditation, refined animations, UI improvements, a looting rework, refreshed motion blur, new accessibility features, a tutorial modernization, HDR improvements, a foliage shading rework, ray-tracing improvements, a global lighting reork, new shading model, subsurface scattering, and a new tone mapper.

PlayStation 5 Pro support, plus Xbox Play Anywhere and unspecified Nintendo Switch 2 "exclusive features" were also mentioned, as were Nvidia DLSS 4.5, AMD FSR 4, Intel XESS 2.0, path tracing and ray reconstruction on PC, native DX12 and rendering parallelization. There will even be ray-traced hair.

Yesterday it was confirmed that Songs of the Past will contain more Gwent , the franchise's compulsive card game.

As previously confirmed, there was no sign of The Witcher 4 tonight — though none was expected. Yesterday, we gained confirmation that the highly-anticipated Ciri-starring sequel is targeting a 2028 release window, and was very much still in the oven at present.

"Our team here at CD Projekt Red HQ is hard at work on a brand new saga, one with Ciri at the helm," CD Projekt Red joint CEO Michał Nowakowski said previously. "We have more than 500 incredibly talented developers working to create something truly special for you. The Witcher 4 features a huge and immersive open world, intense and action-packed gameplay, and a deep, impactful story that we hope will stay with you for a long time. Simply put, this is our biggest, boldest, and most ambitious game to date.

"Now I know you're eager to learn when it's coming. That's the question we're hearing from you all the time. So while we're not showing The Witcher 4 at the event, and we're not ready to share an exact date, I can tell you this: The Witcher 4 is targeting a 2028 release window.

"I know it's a bit of a wait and you'd love to play it sooner, but let the team cook. It will be worth the wait. Until then, there will be plenty more of The Witcher to come, including Songs of the Past when it launches in 2027. And you can be sure gamescom is also in our plans for the coming years."

Catch up on all of tonight's announcements in our roundup of everything revealed at Gamescom Opening Night Live 2026 .

articles.title: Final Fantasy 7 Revelation Gets New Trailer at Gamescom 2026 Showing off Submarine Combat, Weapons, and More
articles.summary: Fans were treated to a new Final Fantasy 7 Revelation trailer at Gamescom’s Opening Night Live showcase, where we saw more of The Weapons, submarine combat, and more.
articles.body:
Fans were treated to a new Final Fantasy 7 Revelation trailer at Gamescom’s Opening Night Live showcase, where we saw more of The Weapons, a submarine combat section, and more.

The trailer opens up with Rufus Shinra sharing a public service announcement on the Shinra News Network regarding the looming Meteor and the Weapons, assuring citizens that humanity will “reign supreme” over these obstacles.

We get to see one of these Weapons wreaking havoc on Shinra soldiers, as well as special shots of the Ruby Weapon, Emerald Weapon, and the Ultima Weapon.

Gameplay footage showing Tifa wearing the Black Mage class outfit was is shown off, as well as a prerendered cutscene showing the Highwind facing off with a Weapon. We even get to see the inside of the submarine with the Huge Materia smack in the middle, along with an underwater combat section that shows the party navigating through the ocean as the submarine dodges attacks.

Footage of the team parachuting down from the Highwind and riding chocobos through the world is also included, as well as Yuffie exploring what seems to be Wutai, making for an extremely hype trailer that is leaving fans more excited than ever.

Most of the dialogue in the trailer centered around the Weapons, with Vincent Valentine explaining in a voiceover that "the Planet sees us as another threat to her well-being, and rightfully so."

"You call 'em planetary warriors," Cid says. "But I call 'em weapons of mass destruction!"

Final Fantasy VII Revelation Screenshots

It remains to be seen if these featured Weapons will be normal bosses or super bosses, in keeping with the original game. Unfortunately, no specific release date was revealed, either. Spring 2027 is still the ongoing release window for the game, which will release simultaneously on PlayStation 5, Nintendo Switch 2, Xbox Series X|S, and PC (via Steam, Epic Games Store, and Xbox PC.

This is the latest look we've gotten at FFVII Revelation following the trailers that were shown at Summer Game Fest earlier this year, where we were reintroduced to the Highwind. Using the airship, Cloud and company will be able to traverse all across the planet, dropping down via parachutes to explore to your heart's content.

It also introduced the FITS system, which allows each character to change their playstyle based on Final Fantasy jobs. Speaking of gameplay, yes, you'll get the chance to play the gunslinging Vincent Valentine and even transform into the Galian Beast.

As yet, not much else has been revealed about the game, but director Naoki Hamaguchi has publicly stated that he wants to integrate many of the Final Fantasy VII spin-off properties into its ultimate ending.

articles.title: Sea of Remnants Director Reveals 10 Minutes of Exclusive Gameplay, Details the Game’s Hidden Secrets
articles.summary: Watch 10 exclusive minutes of Sea of Remnants gameplay as the game's creative director details the RPG's roguelike structure, dice mechanics, and hidden secrets.
articles.body:
When Sea of Remnants releases next year, it promises a free-to-play role playing experience where you’ll be able to both hit the open water on a variety of swashbuckling turn-based missions and explore land-based missions in the game’s fictional setting of Orbtopia. And now, after the release of a brand-new trailer during gamescom 2026’s Opening Night Live, IGN can exclusively reveal more than 10 minutes of gameplay, which you can see in the player above.

Sea of Remnants is being developed by Joker Studios and published by NetEase Games, who recently recently-announced a closed beta test coming this December. Ahead of Opening Night Live, I sat down with the game’s Creative Director, who goes by the name Alfie, to break down the new gameplay and dive into what secrets await for players when the game comes out in 2027.

Sea of Remnants Creative Director breaks down new exclusive gameplay and the game’s mechanics

IGN: What specific mechanics or moments in the exclusive gameplay should we be paying the most attention to?

Alfie: There are three elements that I believe are particularly distinctive. First is the game’s roguelike structure. By combining roguelike progression with turn-based combat and dice mechanics, battles become filled with unpredictability and possibility. We also hope players will pay attention to the music as they experience the game. We have put considerable thought into creating distinct musical atmospheres for voyages at sea, exploration across the islands, combat, and many other situations. Finally, each week, players may discover a new crew member within the world of Sea of Remnants. We want each reunion during a Forgotten Voyage to feel like finding one of your companions all over again. At the same time, every additional crew member introduces new team compositions and combinations, making the roguelike loop richer and opening up even more possibilities.

IGN: What is one mechanic or surprise in Sea of Remnants that you think will genuinely catch players off guard?

Alfie: Sea of Remnants is filled with small details and hidden interactions that we hope players will discover for themselves. For example, if you come across an unassuming lounge chair somewhere in the open world, try sitting down. For a moment, you may forget everything else and simply enjoy the peace and quiet. If I had to choose one genuine surprise, however, it would be the opportunity to discover a crew member each week. Sometimes I may be hoping to find Crew Member A, only to encounter Crew Member B instead. That may disrupt my original plan, but it can also open up entirely new possibilities.

IGN: What does the dual ocean and land settings mean for world-building?

Alfie : Creating an ocean-fantasy world has undoubtedly been one of our greatest challenges. The genre is inherently mysterious, and everyone has their own idea of what it might look like. We spent a long time considering how to distinguish our game and build an original, convincing world, which led us to develop an extensive history and mythology to give the setting depth and internal logic.

Our islands, for example, are designed to feel as authentic and believable as possible, supported by details such as a full 24-hour day-and-night cycle. As players explore the islands and towns, we want them to feel that these are real, lived-in places. Within that grounded world, they will also encounter many strange and imaginative elements; but everything exists naturally within the setting and follows its own consistent logic.

IGN: The game operates on a "set sail, explore, collect, return" rhythm. How does Orbtopia function as part of this loop?

Alfie: Orbtopia plays a central role in this loop. The game is divided into two interconnected layers: the ever-changing voyages at sea and Orbtopia, the safe haven of this ocean world. Players repeatedly set sail from the city and return with the spoils of their adventures. The bounty sent back during a voyage can be put to use in Orbtopia to develop your crew, upgrade your ship, and strengthen your overall capabilities. This progression allows you to venture farther, overcome more difficult challenges, and return with even greater rewards on future voyages.

IGN: With the game’s turn-based combat, how players will need to adapt from one run to the next?

Alfie: To support a wide variety of builds, our combat system needed to accommodate a large number of skills and a meaningful degree of randomness. After extensive testing and iteration, we ultimately chose turn-based combat because it allows us to fully express the freedom and variety of the game’s roguelike build system.

We have also integrated roguelike elements directly into the turn-based combat system, including a dice mechanic that can grant characters an additional action. This adds unpredictability to each encounter while creating more opportunities for strategic decision-making and interactions between different mechanics. Once players reach a certain level, some weaker enemies can be defeated through simplified real-time combat instead. This allows players to focus more of their attention on major boss encounters and exploring the wider world.

IGN: How do you strike a balance between roguelike elements and a longer progression system?

Alfie: Voyage-specific builds provide a faster and more dramatic sense of growth within each run, while progression in Orbtopia establishes a lasting foundation. During each voyage, players can shape their team through a variety of build choices, creating powerful combinations and synergies. These choices are varied and flexible, ensuring that every voyage carries an element of uncertainty. However, a team’s performance at sea is also built upon the permanent progression achieved in Orbtopia. If players encounter an especially difficult opponent, they can return to the city to strengthen their characters’ core abilities, better preparing them for future challenges in the wider world.

Sea of Remnants Creative Director confirms the game will feature customization and accommodate various play styles

IGN: How will the game accommodate different playstyles?

Alfie: Players can follow the main story to explore our major islands at a steady pace. Along the way, they will learn about the characters, discover the nature of this world, and experience the details that make it feel rich and believable. Alternatively, players can embark on the Forgotten Voyage, quickly identify their next objective, and head directly into a new challenge. There are many different ways to experience the game, and players can choose what suits them at any given moment.

Alfie: We believe emotional attachment develops naturally through repeated voyages and the time players spend refining and mastering each character. Using the same crew member across different classes and builds can produce entirely different combat styles. Discovering those possibilities and making them work creates a sense of accomplishment shared between the player and the character, while also deepening the player’s understanding of that crew member. We are also continuing to expand each character’s story and related content, giving players more opportunities to form lasting connections with their crew beyond combat and progression.

IGN: How do player decisions during an expedition affect the narrative and the world around them?

Alfie : The decisions players make in Orbtopia can have a tangible impact on the city and its inhabitants. For example, players may drive certain people away or even cause the city to fall into decline. During the roguelike voyages at sea, decisions are more focused on how players develop their builds. Different combinations of skills and abilities can lead to dramatically different outcomes, shaping how each voyage unfolds.

IGN: When Sea of Remnants comes out next year, what do you expect player reaction to be?

Alfie: Our goal is for players to find joy and entertainment in the game while discovering an immersive and believable ocean world through exploration. Creating a world that feels authentic and convincing has always been deeply important to us.

Sea of Remnants is coming to Android, iOS, PC, PlayStation 5, and XBOX Series X|S in 2027.

articles.title: Some Razer Gaming Gear Is Getting (Slightly Different) Translucent Green Options for Xbox's 25th Anniversary

articles.title: The Witcher 3 Songs of the Past Expansion: Everything Revealed at gamescom ONL 2026
articles.summary: The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Songs of the Past expansion got a proper reveal trailer at gamescom Opening Night Live 2026, and developer CD Projekt Red showed up to talk about its new chain weapon, the realm of Letten, and more.
articles.body:
The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Songs of the Past got a proper reveal trailer at gamescom Opening Night Live 2026, and developer CD Projekt Red showed up to talk about its new chain weapon, the realm of Letten, and more.

Geralt of Rivia helped close out ONL 2026 when the studio talked about how it plans to revisit its critically acclaimed 2015 RPG with new content next year. There's still much that hasn't been revealed, but this first showing finally teased what it will be like for players to revisit The Witcher 3 12 years after its original launch.

We'll get into all of the details that CD Projekt Red had to share, but first, the show had another surprise for viewers: a trailer. You can see the first The Witcher 3 Songs of the Past teaser below.

So, what does the first Songs of the Past trailer tell us? Unfortunately, not much – at least at first glance. Geralt can first be seen approaching a tree decorated with lanterns before dancing in a camp with a partner who may not actually be there. Next, we're introduced to the moonlit skies and sun-kissed fields of Letten, the new realm where Songs of the Past takes place.

Geralt will find himself confronted with a new assortment of humans and monsters, and while that might be nothing new for a Witcher, the big bad whispering throughout the teaser might be. What might have most Witcher 3 fans the most excited, though, is the weapon featured toward the end of the video. The few seconds of footage showed Geralt using a chain to grapple and grapple an enemy before decapitating them. It looks like it could have been ripped right out of the hands of Mortal Kombat's Scorpion and seems to fit well in a Witcher's arsenal.

An official description for the expansion teased what lies in Letten and its ties to the new story: "This idyllic land is rich in rural tradition and folklore, and its people enjoy a fulfilling life of bountiful harvests and lavish festivals. But a dark secret lurks just beneath the surface, and Geralt must overcome never-before-seen foes as he fights to overcome its long-dormant evil."

As revealed during the show, fans can officially wishlist Songs of the Past ahead of its eventual release. CD Projekt Red said the content will take players to the new realm of Letten, though what few sneak peeks we got of it seem to be tied to that trailer.

The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Songs of the Past gamescom ONL 2026 Teaser Trailer - Screenshots

CD Projekt Red Talks Returning to The Witcher 3

Fans of The Witcher games and books will surely find plenty to pick apart while we wait for Songs of the Past to launch next year, but CD Projekt Red didn't want to stop there. Level design lead Miles Tost took the gamescom ONL stage to share more details about how the expansion builds on the original game.

"It's super cool," Tost said with a laugh. "We had this idea for one more story with Geralt for a while, but we couldn't quite figure out how to fit it into our busy schedules. Luckily, our friends from Fool's Theory came around, and they hired a bunch of old veteran Witcher 3 developers – including my mentor, Peter Gelenscer – and here we are today."

Tost noted that this is The Witcher 3 protagonist's last adventure before Ciri takes the torch in The Witcher 4 sometime in 2028 . Giving Geralt a chain will help make his journey in Songs of the Past particularly memorable.

Chains from the books are back, i can't believe this man 😭😭😭😭😭😭😭😭 pic.twitter.com/FXVYm6GEW9 — Kercy (@KdeKercy) August 25, 2026

Chains from the books are back, i can't believe this man 😭😭😭😭😭😭😭😭 pic.twitter.com/FXVYm6GEW9

"This chain is a weapon that is new in the game, but many people, perhaps hardcore Witcher fans, will realize that this is a weapon we first showed in The Witcher 1 intro," Tost continued, directing fans to head to the CD Projekt Red booth at gamescom to learn more.

Tost also had some words to share about Letten and how that environment will change things up for fans: "Letten is a whole new, unique region that has a unique identity, like the other regions in the game. It is filled with quests, new monsters, adventures and exploration – just like the things that Witcher fans love. But it's an almost uncannily idyllic place that, however, has a dark secret lurking just underneath the surface and, as it is a Witcher game, this kind of secret requires a true professional Witcher to solve."

Geralt is finally back. The Witcher 3 Songs of the Past may not have a release date, but it is still expected to launch sometime in 2027 for PC, Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X|S. In the meantime, players can also look forward to The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered , which was also announced during gamescom ONL 2026.

We'll hopefully learn more about the surprise expansion in the months ahead. In the meantime, the developer also recently confirmed that the add-on will bring more Gwent to the game . You can also check out everything announced during ONL here .

The Apple Airtags is a practical accessory for iPhone owners who tend to lose small wearables like wallets, keys, cats, or remotes.

articles.title: Konami Partners With Celebrity Kitty to Release Metal Gear Cat Toys at CatCon 2026
articles.summary: Konami is partnering up with a celebrity kitty named ‘one-eared Uno’ to debut a special Metal Gear cat toy collection available at CatCon 2026.
articles.body:
Konami is partnering up with a celebrity kitty named ‘one-eared Uno’ to debut a special Metal Gear cat toy collection available at CatCon 2026.

If you didn’t know there was a cat convention, now you do. CatCon is a yearly event that brings together cat lovers from all over the globe to Pasadena, California, featuring special exhibits, workshops, adoption drives, and meet-and-greets with celebrity cats.

One of those cats, affectionately named ‘one-eared Uno,’ and her owner, Kat Curtis, will host a special meet-and-greet event at the Konami booth at CatCon this year to celebrate the release of some special Metal Gear-themed cat toys.

These offerings include cat scratch boxes modeled after the iconic cardboard boxes that Big Boss and Old Snake use to sneak around without being detected by enemies, plush pet toys, and even cat collars inspired by Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker and Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots .

The lovable one-eared Uno with her adorable underbite was rescued by Kat as a stray, who found the kitty abandoned near a dumpster. The two now boast over five million followers on social media and are meeting fans at Catcon on October 12 at 2 PM PST.

CatCon takes place at the Pasadena Convention Center from October 10 - 11. Cat lovers will be able to score the Snake-approved merch for their kitties on those days only, both at the convention and online via the OKS Gear Shop.

What’s more, fans can win a chance to meet Uno at CatCon and get the exclusive Metal Gear merch if they visit the Konami booth at the convention and either: show they own the Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2, add the collection to their wishlist, or purchase the Metal Gear merchandise at the booth.

This collaboration might be off the wall, but given the sheer amount of absurdities that take place within the series, we can’t say that this partnership is totally out of left field. This limited-time partnership marks the launch of the Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 , a compilation of the classic stealth-action games that releases on August 17, 2026 for Nintendo Switch, Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, XBOX Series X|S, and Steam.

articles.title: Ridley Scott Knows How to Make a Good Post-Apocalyptic Movie, but Unfortunately, The Dog Stars Is Not One of Them
articles.summary: Ridley Scott's post-apocalyptic survivor drama keeps its feelings about grieving in a triple layer of emotional bubble wrap.
articles.body:
The Dog Stars releases in theaters August 28.

Ridley Scott is hardly a novice when it comes to depicting determined men (and occasionally women) shouldering various degrees of emotional repression while doing whatever it takes to survive in hostile spaces. Really, take your pick from a career that spans nearly 50 years. More often than not, his films resonate — he’s earned the right to call himself an “influencer,” however ridiculous the quote. But his latest, The Dog Stars, which has seemed to catch the general public flat-footed, is a miss that’s too many steps removed from its emotional center to find any fresh truth in the crowded post-apocalyptic survival genre.

The Dog Stars, based on the 2012 Peter Heller novel, is not necessarily the tense action-thriller about a man (Jacob Elordi), his dog, and the unlikely ratio of hot people fighting to stay alive in a lawless, overgrown dystopia that the trailer makes it out to be. Instead, it’s largely a slow-moving survival story set years after a strange virus decimates society, leaving behind said hot people to grieve while a whole other subset of remaining people seemingly loses their minds, banding together to become violently deranged hordes who live to loot from those who are trying to keep a peaceful existence. Requisite lonesome acoustic guitar soundtrack straight from The Last of Us included, of course, along with a few other baffling country music needle drops.

The first 20 minutes alone are an extended side quest following Elordi’s mechanic Hig and his good boy Jasper on a supply run, loping through an abandoned Denver for Coca Cola products and medical supplies amid unquestionably gorgeous wide shots of the city. Hig flies through Rocky Mountain forests in his tiny yellow prop jet, his signature move being to kill the engine and just coast above it all with Jasper in the co-pilot seat, listening for a radio signal from a place called Grand Junction that’s rumored to harbor the last vestiges of civilization. It’s perfectly suited for IMAX, which is how I saw The Dog Stars. But these recurring vistas feel like excuses to shoot this for the premium screen experience using the nature cheat code, despite this being a film that would have otherwise crushed on streaming, where people aren’t captive audiences and might not be forced to feel too deeply or think about basic world-building questions, such as: What’s the deal with this mysterious killer flu anyway? How did those looters turn so feral? How does Hig still have a full supply of coffee beans (and does he have French Roast)?

It’s not entirely that this movie is patently uninterested in the society that came before, but it is more focused on how those who remain cope with the present, content to reminisce over their past lives in dull conversations. When Hig returns from his supply run to the homestead he shares with Josh Brolin’s hardened (and occasionally funny) ex-Marine Bangley, the two quibble over being happy with what they have and how best to lock down their property from the threat of the looters they call Reapers that need to be “dealt with like roaches.” (Bristling bros, very hot right now !) Hig journeys out and finds his way to the father-daughter duo Jack (Guy Pearce, also doing an occasionally funny grumbly paranoid dad) and Cima (a perfectly serviceable Margaret Qualley). As they pull up tree stumps and sit under the stars together, Cima and Hig talk about their dead spouses. Hig flirts with her by talking about… golf. The Dog Stars script, written by Mark L. Smith, is the film’s dead weight, full of leaden dialogue that’s fine in a novel and sounds wildly contrived coming out of a real person’s mouth.

After a sleepy first hour, things pick up with coinciding standoffs of our central characters — Hig, Cima, and Jack in their neck of the woods, Bangley holding down his compound — vs. the Reapers, where we finally get a taste of the guns-blazing action promised in the trailer. In a stylish first-person sequence, Bangley, going full military ops mode, dons a night vision monocular that turns people into smearing neon green and their blood into proverbial paintball splatter. Hig and co. need to outrun a reaper pincer maneuver that ends with the first shock-laugh of the movie. These moments are, as you’d expect, exciting and well-directed, but the question of what are the intruders even doing hangs over these scenes. I don’t need every single character motivation explained — abstraction can be great! — but the lack of anything beyond “these are the bad guys consumed by inscrutable runes” who are depicted as whooping shirtless tattooed fiends is, speaking generously, not from this era of filmmaking. All of this does lead to a wild third-act shift that has some verve when the Hig trio reaches Grand Junction, headlined by Allison Janney doing the most capital-A acting of the whole movie in a ‘50s stewardess getup.

I can’t discuss a movie called The Dog Stars without talking more about Jasper the dog. As in any movie with a trusty companion, I brace myself for whatever may come , hoping for the best yet expecting emotional terrorism. But, like every other connection in this movie, even man’s best pal is kept at a somewhat icy emotional distance. For all the jostling to reckon with the sheer amount of societal loss, it all ends up feeling like something to shrug off — even the stuff with the dog. Oh well, at least we have The Sheep Detectives .

articles.title: Showa American Story: The First Hands-On Preview
articles.summary: Showa American Story succeeds in crafting an unforgettable, eccentric B-movie world. However, its deliberate jank and niche style mean its general polish still lags behind other modern AAA action games at this point. The sheer density of cultural parodies is impressive, but whether the game can sustain this tone over a dozens-of-hours-long campaign without exhausting players remains to be seen. Coupled with its current shortcomings in combat depth and mechanical feel, Showa American Story is shaping up to be an incredibly unique, highly flawed, yet undeniably fascinating ride.
articles.body:
Showa's delightfully odd take on pop culture makes it unique.

Combat depth and mechanical feel are lacking in its present state.

Showa American Story is, if nothing else, a profoundly wacky action-RPG. Five years have passed since its initial reveal in 2021, and with barely any updates in recent years, players have been left wondering: In an era where the Chinese AAA single-player market is rapidly expanding, can a game with such an eccentric tone actually carve out its own identity?

We recently had the chance to go hands-on with about two hours of Showa American Story. Based on an introduction by Creative Director Xiangyu Luo and our own gameplay experience, here is what makes this absurd adventure tick. Luo describes Showa American Story as an RPG overflowing with retro pop culture. Set in an alternate late-'80s where Japan bought up most of the United States, effectively colonizing it economically and culturally, players take control of Choko Chigusa—a girl brought back from the dead. She embarks on a road trip filled with combat, exploration, and growth across a world that feels both absurdly bizarre and weirdly familiar.

Our demo was split into four segments: a linear story-and-combat section, a camp exploration slice focused on rest and character progression, an open-map exploration sequence, and a massive boss fight.

Combat in Showa American Story integrates elements from various action game staples, as Choko can use both melee and ranged weapons. The demo featured four types of melee weapons—Bare Hands/Gauntlets, Katanas, Drills, and Polearms—alongside ranged options like shotguns and assault rifles. Every melee weapon comes with a specific name. For instance, the katana category consists entirely of historical legendary blades; I found one called "Mikazuki Munechika" lying around. You can actually equip it, though the item description hilariously notes it's probably just a fake.

Weapon categories boast intensely edgy, anime-style move names and wildly different playstyles: Bare Hands: Beyond basic fists, you can equip gauntlets, brass knuckles, and even "Wolf Fang Vajra Claws"—which look exactly like Wolverine's iconic claws. They offer the highest attack speed, but naturally, the lowest damage. Katana: This category has the deepest moveset. Depending on your light and heavy attack combos, Choko shifts into different "Stances" (Kamae), offering branching attack paths for your next move. Light + Heavy triggers "High Stance," Light + Light + Heavy initiates "Yin-Yang Stance," and a single Heavy attack results in "Matsukaze Stance." There's even a long combo (four Lights, three Heavies) that unleashes a "Reversed Hasso Stance" capable of parrying, while double Heavy puts you in a "Fudoshin (Immovable Mind) Stance." Polearms: The demo let us wield a literal American flag as a dual-handed weapon. It excels at wide-sweeping attacks and grants Super Armor. While it struggles to instantly break enemies, it easily knocks them down. The trade-off is massive stamina consumption, which can be mitigated through upgrades. And Drills: Harder to master. The attacks are mostly linear and restrict your ability to sprint, but the damage is astronomical. The linear thrusts pierce through enemies, and using a Rage Attack drastically shortens the weapon's long wind-up animation while leaving a lingering cyclone for continuous multi-hit damage.

The core of the combat revolves around a strategic "Rage Cycle." Dealing or taking damage builds the Rage meter. Once enough is gathered, it converts into a "Rage Point" (currently capped at 5). Weapon types generate Rage at drastically different rates; barehanded weapons build it the fastest. Therefore, swapping to fists when you're starved for resources is the optimal play. Even within a category, there are nuances—gauntlets deal less damage than brass knuckles but build Rage faster.

Rage Points dictate the flow of combat and can be spent in several ways: Ultimates: Consume multiple points for massive damage (3 points for barehanded, 5 points for katanas). Rage Attacks: Holding R1 and pressing Triangle turns your standard heavy attack into a stronger Rage variant. Katanas gain extended reach, while Drills inflict longer sustained damage. Chain Attacks: Similar to the "Flash Attack" in the Nioh series. Pressing R1 and the D-pad corresponding to another melee weapon during an attack consumes 1 Rage Point to instantly swap weapons and unleash a high-damage follow-up with zero recovery frames. Swapping to a firearm triggers Bullet Time and exposes enemy weak points. Standard weapon swapping is notoriously slow, making Chain Attacks the most effective way to juggle your arsenal. Perfect Dodge & Super Recovery: Holding R1 + Dodge at any time spends 1 point for a Perfect Dodge; subsequently pressing the attack button unleashes a Melee Chain or Ranged Chain. Alternatively, getting hit by a heavy attack triggers a brief slow-motion window; pressing dodge here burns 1 point for a "Super Recovery," and pressing attack immediately after automatically fires off a Melee Counter or Ranged Counter.

Rage and Chain attacks quickly deplete an enemy's stamina. Once they are broken, you can perform an Execution. Thus, the ideal combat loop looks like this: quickly build Rage, spend it for high damage or Ultimates, but always keep 1 point in the tank to seamlessly swap back to fists to rebuild your meter. It requires intense focus and resource management.

Alongside Rage, Stamina deeply impacts the pacing. Regular light attacks consume Stamina (especially heavy weapons like the flag). Since Showa often throws Dynasty Warriors-sized hordes at you, this stamina cost can feel restricting early on. However, the stamina penalty isn't overly harsh. Running out of stamina doesn't leave you paralyzed; instead, it drops your defense, causing you to take significantly more damage. Interestingly, this loops back into the Rage Cycle: landing a Rage Attack restores Stamina. So, mindless button-mashing will get you killed. You have to weave Rage Attacks into your combos before your stamina depletes to stay healthy.

That said, the combat feel and enemy interactions are currently quite rough. First, the hit-stop on melee strikes is overly pronounced, making the combat feel sluggish rather than impactful. Second, there's very little actual interaction between the player and enemies—it often feels like both sides are just swinging through each other. Choko has very low poise and gets staggered easily, yet enemy attack timings are incredibly difficult to read. The Perfect Dodge window is especially baffling; sometimes you need to dodge before an attack even connects, and other times it feels like you have to get hit first to trigger it.

Showa American Story - Exclusive Art and Screenshots

These clunky interactions often derail the "Rage Cycle." Because enemy attacks are unpredictable, players tend to panic-roll when hit. This accidentally triggers Super Recoveries, instantly draining your hard-earned Rage meter and putting you on the back foot. Furthermore, the game’s visual presentation—particularly blood and combat effects—can be overwhelming to the point of distraction, leading to visual and operational experiences that are currently a bit underwhelming.

On the RPG side, Showa American Story features a robust progression system. You earn XP to level up in real-time. Core stats include Health, Stamina, Rage, Defense, Melee, and Shooting; leveling up automatically increases these stats while granting BP (Battle Points) to unlock character skills.

Weapons have six detailed stats: Base Power, Rage Generation, Break Application, Crit Rate, Crit Multiplier, and Stamina Consumption. You can upgrade them up to level five using in-game currency (US Dollars) and upgrade parts. Upgrading provides clear, flat-percentage damage boosts, and weapons currently feature seven buff slots. You can equip accessories for further stat boosts and change outfits—though be warned, most are highly revealing.

Showa American Story - August 2026 Screenshots

Your base of operations, meanwhile, is an RV named "Guren." Pressing R3 switches to a first-person view to explore the camp, talk to companions, or decorate. Showa uses an AP (Action Point) system. You earn AP by doing almost anything in the world (looting, talking to NPCs, etc.) and spend it back at the RV on activities like drinking soda, working out, or taking a bath. These activities grant XP for your Melee and Rage stats, and build resistances to eight status effects (burn, shock, poison, etc.). Funnily enough, all daily activities require specific base facilities and consumables—like a bathtub and bath salts for bathing—which you have to find or buy yourself.

Visually, while character models and facial animations are a bit stiff (which might actually be an intentional stylistic choice), the environmental detail in the demo was fantastic. The foliage, water, and rocks at a hot spring inn looked incredibly realistic, and a mountain climbing section up Neo Yokohama was dripping with nostalgic atmosphere. The open-map shopping streets are meticulously designed, packed with NPCs, and different shops sell unique items and weapons. You can even find your companions on the street to soak your feet together, increasing your max HP.

The story’s tone rivals the wackiest substories in the Yakuza series, blending dark humor with internet memes (both Chinese and international) and absurd concepts like a "Zombie Human Rights Association." Even the difficulty settings are a joke (in a good way): "Heisei Loser" for Normal, and "Showa Boy" for Hard. Some cutscenes use a PPT-style slideshow presentation similar to Yakuza 0—static poses with voice acting but no lip-sync. However, the camera work and pacing here are so deliberate that it clearly aims to emulate the vibe of a retro B-movie.

To sell the era, the developers clearly spent a fortune on art assets and music licensing. The combat and RV exploration tracks are heavily Showa-inspired, and one demo segment even featured Hiromi Go’s Japanese cover of "Casablanca" (Aishuu no Casablanca). The boss fights are as bizarre as they are gory; one encounter on a waterfall suspension bridge suddenly shifts the perspective into a 2D side-scrolling brawler where guns are disabled, and the fourth segment's lengthy boss fight interspersed chase sequences between combat phases. After surviving this absurd encounter, the game played an original ending song with lyrics by director Xiangyu Luo and vocals by Japanese singer Mayu Wakisaka. Additionally, there are fully playable retro arcade cabinets paying homage to Space Harrier and Sega's classic OutRun, showcasing an impressive volume of bespoke art and music.

Ultimately, Showa American Story succeeds in crafting an unforgettable, eccentric B-movie world. However, its deliberate jank and niche style mean its general polish still lags behind other modern AAA action games at this point. The sheer density of cultural parodies is impressive, but whether the game can sustain this tone over a dozens-of-hours-long campaign without exhausting players remains to be seen. Coupled with its current shortcomings in combat depth and mechanical feel, Showa American Story is shaping up to be an incredibly unique, highly flawed, yet undeniably fascinating ride.

articles.title: Toxic: A Fairy Tale for Grown-Ups Is a Lavish But Incomprehensible Action Epic Featuring Megastar Yash
articles.summary: Toxic: A Fairy Tale for Grown-Ups review: A sloppy gangster epic finds Indian megastar Yash in the mood for blood.
articles.body:
Toxic: A Fairy Tale for Grown-Ups will be released on August 26.

A gangland action saga spread across five decades, Toxic: A Fairy Tale for Grown-Ups runs 194 minutes but plays like a trailer for something else. While it’s technically a complete story — a rarity in the modern South Indian blockbuster landscape, where every other major release is actually a “Part 1” — the film is edited with the kind of snappy impressionism that becomes completely disorienting when you need to make sense of who’s who, or quite simply who’s standing where. Granted, the presence of bearded A-lister Yash of the KGF duology (often credited as “Rocking Star” Yash) goes a long way toward making it tolerable at times. The actor has layered charisma and explosiveness in his dual roles as ruthless mafioso Raya, and eventually his spurned son Rumi or “Ticket,” who seeks revenge for his abandonment. However, making sense of Toxic visually and narratively is a major challenge.

On the plus side, Toxic has a visual splendor given its period setting. The story runs from the 1920s all the way through India’s independence in 1947, and even goes a few decades further, tracing the changing face of the former Portuguese port of Goa as a reimagined haven for a heightened drug trade awash in slick suits, fedoras, tommy guns, and lavish speakeasies. It’s India’s western coast by way of 1920s Chicago, a fanciful façade that makes Toxic among the most expensive Indian movies ever made (certainly the most expensive one released thus far; it’s out-spent only by S.S. Rajamouli’s RRR follow-up, Varanasi, arriving in April, and the Hindu epic Ramayana: Part 1, also starring Yash and releasing in November). Alas, all this effort feels wasted on a completely unfocused movie whose soul resides in its opening and closing minutes but whose intervening three hours are a headache and a half.

Opening at a circus in medias res, Toxic finds a young boy nicknamed Ticket (his face painted like a sad clown) being handed over by his manic acrobat mother, Nadia (Kiara Advani), to his vengeful father, Raya (Yash) — the first of several characters introduced angrily chugging a bottle of booze. This angst-laden intro engenders curiosity; something painful has clearly transpired in these characters’ pasts, setting the stage for an explosive future. But the blanks are soon filled in at lightspeed. The powerplay for Goa’s drug trade, going back several decades, involved Raya’s unseen father alongside several Portuguese gangsters, each with their own family entanglements. Eventually, Raya and his steely older sister, Ganga (Nayanthara), become major players vis-à-vis a series of crisscrossing betrayals.

The film is quick to jump into its action set pieces, which feature blood and violence aplenty as well as the kind of macho heroic posing one might expect from a “pan-India” production emanating from the country’s south, but things go quickly awry. Like many films aimed at multiple markets, Toxic was shot simultaneously in multiple languages — in this case, Kannada and English. The latter version is appropriately flowery for a story touted as a violent fairy tale, but its attempts at poetic dialogue end up simply explaining the meaning and subtext behind the story at hand as characters deliver every line like it’s either a quip or a lofty proclamation. This has a numbing effect: After a while, no bit of dialogue actually stands out.

Equally anesthetic is the litany of breakneck action. For the majority of its runtime, Toxic’s story is told by way of some rival faction or another opening fire on Raya’s crew as he overcomes the odds, but actually tracing who’s who — or why anyone is doing anything at all — is a fool’s errand. You could certainly turn your brain off to the movie’s flip-book unfurling, but watching Toxic might just require you to turn your eyes off from time to time too. The sheer number of cuts with no legible point of focus or geography is disorienting to say the least.

Sadly, the film’s sloppy assembly doesn’t end at its visual construction. Musically, it’s stuck in the early-to-mid aughts, drawing from the soundtracks of international blockbuster and arthouse darlings of the era — In The Mood for Love, Donnie Darko, Requiem for a Dream, even The Dark Knight — without much by way of originality or coherent sonic identity.

Ordinarily, the blame for all this would lie at the feet of the director, but in this case, it’s hard to imagine that Toxic — at least, the completed version now in cinemas — is at all the brainchild of filmmaker Geetu Mohandas. Her last film, the Malayalam-language gangster movie Moothon, masterfully disguised a queer drama steeped in intimate anguish. But even as one of the few women to helm such a major Indian release, it’s hard not to speculate about her actual influence (or lack thereof). Toxic feels like the product of a studio system bowing to tropes in the realm of hero worship and machismo, despite occasional attempts to subvert these expectations, with larger set pieces that depend entirely on misogynistic violence. It gets pretty gross on occasion, in a manner designed to satiate some kind of chauvinistic blood lust.

Yash’s Raya is defined by philandering and sexist jabs, but the gaze of Mohandas’ camera is markedly shifted from the male-centric lens of Indian mass media. Her focus during both sex and action is hairy chests and rolled-up sleeves instead of oily washboard abs, and her female characters are afforded more bodily dignity than the average heroine. However, these bare minimums don’t amount to much in a story where actually tracing the characters’ relationships is a game of Whac-a-Mole. Actresses like Nayanthara, Advani, Huma Qureshi, Tara Sutaria, and Rukmini Vasanth play women defined by their proximity to male gangsters — I’d list them all, but mapping the tree of the movie’s character dynamics would take several days — and they all eventually oscillate between stoic poise and outright yelling for minutes at a time until the drama becomes too grating to endure.

This aural unpleasantness applies to Yash as well, who consumes the lion’s share of the screen time as both the film’s mournful protagonist as well as his vindictive son. Although Ticket only appears in the final act despite the hopscotching timeline, it’s the rare role for which Yash has a thin goatee instead of a full beard, making him look practically unrecognizable (along with some digital de-aging). But is this enough to dramatically separate Ticket from his father? The answer is more complicated than “yes” or “no.” That both men harbor the same incandescent rage is part of the movie’s point about the cycles of male violence trickling through generations, and together, Yash and Mohandas manage to craft something special with these performances, even if we’re only exposed to glimmers of that brilliance thanks to the haphazard cutting.

As Raya, Yash offers hints of a hidden self-loathing beneath his violent, womanizing exterior, while as Ticket, he creates a unique physicality through a character whose swift parkour motions feel like something out of a fever dream. Amid the movie’s snowy and rainy settings, Ticket is the only human element that feels appropriately heightened beyond the expected limits of Indian action blockbusters. It might be one of Yash’s finest performances to date; unfortunately, it’s stuck in a movie where violence, although serving the thematic purpose of generational trauma, also seems to explode randomly, both from and against characters we’ve never seen before, and whose motives and place within the story are head-scratching to say the least. Ultimately, the result is a banal story that sometimes explodes with jarring noise.
